title: The Boast of a Thousand Arms
subtitle: Vana vaunts, and Krishna answers with the Sarnga bow
story:
"Wait! Wait!" Vana shouted across the field of Sonitpura. "You will not escape me today alive to Dwaraka, to see your friends there. O Madhava, you have been urged on by Death. Vanquished by me in battle, you will look on the golden leaves of the trees on the eve of your death. O Garudhwaja, you have eight arms — how will you fight with me, who have a thousand? Slain with all your friends in the city of Shonita, you will remember Dwaraka. Today you will see my thousand arms, adorned with various weapons and ornaments, multiply into a million."

His words travelled over the field like the dreadful waves of an ocean raised by wind, and his eyes, filled with anger, shone like two suns rising in the firmament.

From the top of the palace, Narada laughed aloud — so loudly that the sky seemed sundered in twain. Seated on his yoga seat, the ascetic moved about on all sides, filled with curiosity to see the battle.

Krishna answered with the patience of a man who had heard many boasts. "O Vana, why do you roar thus out of foolishness? Heroes do not vaunt. What is the use of vaunting? Come and fight with me in the battlefield. O son of Diti, you have given vent to many unconnected words. If victory were accomplished by words in a battle, you would no doubt be victorious already. Come, Vana — either defeat me, or, vanquished by me, lie down on the earth for good, with your face down."

And with that he struck Vana with arrows that cut him to the quick. Vana, in turn, covered Krishna with burning arrows, with parighas and nisthringsas, with clubs, tomars, shaktis, maces and pattishas, until the holder of the conch, the discus and the club was buried beneath them. Proud Vana, with his thousand arms, fought easily; and Keshava, who had eight, fought on. Seeing Krishna's superior training, the son of Bali grew greatly worked up with anger, and he discharged the celestial great weapon that Brahma, by his ascetic powers, had created long ago for Hiranyakashipu. All the quarters were enshrouded with darkness; thousands of dreadful omens appeared on every side; everything went beyond the range of perception. The Danavas applauded Vana — "Well done! Well done!" — while the cries of the gods, "Alas!", were heard. A dreadful downpour of burning arrows was caused by the force of that weapon, and while Keshava was being burnt, wind, storm and clouds did not move.

Then the divine slayer of Madhu took up Indra's weapon, like unto inevitable death. The moment it was ready, all the worlds were shorn of darkness, the fire was extinguished, and the Danavas completely lost their hearts. Seeing their weapon counteracted as soon as Indra's weapon was drawn, the gods began to laugh and roar like lions.

Beside himself with rage, Vana spoke harsh words to Keshava on Garuda's back and covered him with maces and pattishas. Keshava, the slayer of his enemies, counteracted his uplifted weapons, smiling. Then, with arrows like thunderbolts shot from his Sarnga bow, he sundered Vana's car, with its horses and standards, into pieces. The very next moment he separated from Vana's person his lustrous crown, his coat of mail, his bow and his shield — and, smiling, struck him on the breast with winged arrows. Cut to the very quick, Vana lost consciousness and swooned away.

From the top of the palace, Narada rose up clapping. "O great fortune! Great fortune! Blessed is my life and my birth, since I have witnessed today this wonderful prowess of Damodara. O large-armed one, adored by the gods, accomplish that for which you have incarnated yourself — destroy soon Diti's son Vana."

And as the armies watched, even the standards fought their own battle: the horses of the gods and of the Danavas clashed, and Garuda and the peacock struck at each other with wings, beaks and talons, until the great bird, leaping up in anger, seized the peacock's head in his beak.
reflection: Narada's laughter at the boast and his applause at the defeat frame the whole duel as a spectacle: the ascetic watches from the palace rooftop, and the mightiest warriors of the universe perform for him. The hundred arms multiply into a million only in Vana's own telling — in the end, it is one bow that dismantles them.
next_story_tease: But Vana's life was not yet decided — the goddess would step between them once more.
hero_scene: Vana's thousand arms spread in fury as Krishna's arrows from the Sarnga bow shatter his chariot, crown, mail, bow and shield, while Narada claps from the palace rooftop and Garuda battles the peacock overhead.
